newsitem.title: USA: U.S. foreign crude scene in quiet holding pattern.
newsitem.headline: U.S. foreign crude scene in quiet holding pattern.

text.p: U.S. refiners' avoidance of pricey Brent and West African crudes continued Tuesday and even widened in the sense that buying seemed to halt entirely as players sought to get a handle on the market, traders said.

Continuing pressure on the spread between West Texas Intermediate/Cushing and North Sea Brent continued to make the North Sea market altogether too expensive, even though the spread rose 5 seven cents Tuesday to settle at $1.17 a barrel.
"I think it's pretty quiet now with the Brent/WTI spread coming in," said one player.
"There's very little activity. Everyone's trying to determine whether the market is oversupplied," said another trader, noting he was not sure.

He said deals were scarce in the North Sea market, let alone the Gulf Coast which was dead, adding that he could not gauge the signficance of one U.S. player's retraction of an offer this week that was never taken out by a buyer last week.
Much of the waiting and uncertainty centered on weekly petroleum supply, production and demand statistics from the American Petroleum Institute.

Questions ranging from crude import levels to implied gasoline demad weighed on traders boldness, who hoped the report will provide some direction in order that the foreign crude market again breathe life.
The report, which covers developments through last week, is due out later Tuesday afternoon.

In the meanwhile, players continue to look for foreign crudes in Latin America, from where the "usual suspects" were offering among other grades, Colombian Cusiana crude for July loading, traders said.
-- Oliver Ludwig, New York Energy Desk, 1 212 859 1633
